TL;DR: What are the rules on sheathing, drawing, then attacking in one turn? I haven't seen anything so I made a house rule at the bottom of this post

So the question came up regarding one of my PCs, a Barbarian, sheathing his great-axe, drawing two hand-axes, and then being able to use an Attack action and everything else for free. That threw a proverbial flag for me and I went to look it up. I see in the PHB (190) where it mentions *"... or you could draw your weapon as part of the same action you use to attack." *. I also see where it mentions in the same section "If you want to interact with a second object, you need to use your action."

Here's where I have issues. D&D is very particular about how things are worded. Yes, they make errata, but they make sure it's worded exactly how they want it and I haven't seen anything on this, yet. In order, the barb is sheathing, then drawing. I could see the sheathing as part of the "free interaction with an object", but would that then not allow the PC to draw while attacking? Would it then require them to use an action to draw the hand-axes? To me, and maybe you guys can clarify, I feel as if it's overkill (I may be wrong) to require a player to spend an action to either sheathe or draw. Drawing a weapon takes only a second to do. I could see maybe making them spend a Bonus action to either sheathe or draw, but to me a great-axe would require more effort to sheathe than a dagger.

What if I made them spend movement to sheathe? In a sense, all they're doing is moving anyways, right? In fact, what if we considered movement as a resource when the player wants to do stuff that simply requires them to move around? If they had to spend movement to sheathe, then they could use their "free interaction with an object" and draw while attacking. Here's what I came up with.

<Type> = <Cost>

  • Simple Weapons = 5 feet

  • Martial Weapons = 10 feet

  • Contains "Heavy" Property = +5 feet

  • Contains "Reach" Property = +5 feet

  • Contains "Light" Property = -5 feet

Notes:

  • Each player must spend a minimum of 5 feet to sheathe.

  • If a player has a Dexterity equal to 16 or more, the minimum feet required drops to 0. [Changed 15 to 16]

  • If a player has a Dexterity less than 10, he/she must roll a Dexterity check (DC 10). On a fail, the player sheathes incorrectly and drops the weapon.

  • The free "interact with an object" action must be assigned to the weapon with the lowest penalty. [Added]

There may already be something better, but I haven't found it. Please educate me if this is bad or unnecessary. As usual, I'm completely open to constructional criticism.
[Homebrew] Rules On Sheathing One Weapon, Drawing Another, Then Attacking All In One Turn?

From the Dual Wielder feat:

You can draw or stow two one-handed weapons when you would normally be able to draw or stow only one.

Which adds some clarification. As a houserule, I put a price on all "minor" actions after the first with something similar to yours, with just a flat 15 speed per minor action, with the "dash" action being an option to gain access to more minor actions. Using the dash action and sacrificing all of your movement, you can get up to 5 minor actions a turn (with both drawing and sheathing being two different minor actions).

It's simple, it still gives value to the Dual Wielder double draw effect (you don't lose 15 speed on the turn you draw on), and it's something to strategize around. Although your concept of "only allowing a single draw, and separately costing to sheath" is an interesting concept I didn't think about.
I like that idea. I may have incorrectly read your comment, but wouldn't this method also give value to the DW feat?

To be honest, both of our options steal power from the DW feat, since the DW feat is the only option to draw/sheath two weapons at once.

Where mine makes it a possibility to do both (albeit at a hefty cost, with DW allowing a second "free" minor action to draw or sheath), yours makes sheathing any weapon a cost while scaling with the size of the weapon (DW originally allows drawing/sheathing a second weapon for free and allows bigger weapons, meaning larger movement penalties with the feat with your system). Unless your system allows exceptions when using the Dual Wielder feat, the movement penalties are greater while dual wielding (feat included).

What I mean by this is, my homebrew adds options with prices that DW makes cheaper, while your homebrew adds options with prices that DW would require more to spend (since sheathing costs per size and per weapon).

Gotcha. So here's my thought. The way I read the last bullet of DW ("You can draw or stow two one-handed weapons when you would normally be able to draw or stow only one."), they have to be either drawing or stowing both weapons concurrently. For example, Bill has a longsword out. He wants to sheathe it and dual-wield hand-axes. All three are one-handed, but by my house rule, the longsword would cost 10 feet where a hand-axe would cost 5 feet (10 feet since there are two if he didn't have DW). He decides to assign his longsword and one hand-axe to the two weapons he uses for DW, making him only have to pay 5 feet for one of the hand-axes. No says I. The free second weapon is required to be the one being dual-wielded, which means he'd have to pay 10 feet for stowing the longsword.

If the situation is reversed and he has the two hand-axes out, but he wants his longsword, then he'd only have to pay 5 feet to stow the hand-axes, instead of 10 feet since it's two weapons and he has DW, and then the longsword would be free since it's part of his attack action.

Either way, he's paying for at least one of the weapons. Does that make sense or did I not understand your comment?

Not quite the point I was trying to make, but I understand what you're trying to make happen.

With yours, only sheathing has a cost while drawing has a flat limit based off of whether or not you have DW (1 if you don't, 2 if you do). If you don't, and you sheath, you spend it for each individual weapon. If you do, you can stow at the cost of the first weapon, but the second weapon you stow is free.

My issue is, the DW feat allows for larger weapons to be used (is no longer restricted to light weapons), but your system penalizes non-light weapons (effectively saying that if you want to go DW and expect this system to work inf your favor, guess again).

What I didn't realize from before is that this is off-balanced by the fact that, in your system, the second stowed weapon is free. So if I go from two handaxes without DW (two light weapons, stow cost of 5 each, for a total of 10 to stow) to two normal, martial weapons (10 to stow for each, but the second one is free, for a total of 10 to stow) it is exactly the same.

It's an interesting concept, just be aware that it might complicate some of the 'simpler' parts of combat. Whether or not you consider that a good thing is up to you.

Maybe I've miscommunicated something or I'm not following you. Drawing the second wouldn't be free if the player doesn't have DW. Only the first would be, which means they'd be paying for the second draw, which makes sense to me. Since they also had to pay for stowing the other two, if they happen to come out to the same cost, so be it, I guess. They paid for it, so to me it doesn't matter.

I think I just misunderstood.

I thought that, with your system, drawing a weapon doesn't have any cost tied to it, only stowing does. On top of that, if you have the DW feat your second draw and stow is free (as long as the weapons are different).

Did I make a mistake? Or maybe this has just gotten way too complicated...?

The system would be for both drawing and sheathing. The free "interact with object" action uses drawing a weapon as an example. I think maybe that's were we both kept getting confused. IDK. lol. Really, they should be able to assign the free "interact with object" action to any of the weapons, but I added that they'd have to assign the it to the weapon with the lowest penalty. Otherwise they'd be able to say, "I want to use my free action to sheathe my great-axe and then spend speed to draw my hand-axes". That'd only cost them 10 feet where the great-axe would cost 15 + the hand-axe which would come to 20 feet. No says I. I could see using a free action to draw or stow the lightest thing you had, but the heaviest? Nah. Does that clear it up any?
